Upon no objections to Proposed Order issued on September 15, 1995, following a
hearing held before Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) David W. Stiteler on August 23,
1995, in Salem, Oregon. After the hearing, the case was administratively reassigned to
ALJ Susan Rossiter for preparation of a recommended decision.
Richard R. Trotts, P.O. Box 156, Stayton, Oregon 97383, appeared prose.
Gary M. Cordy, Assistant Attorney General, Labor and Employment Section,
Department of Justice, 100 Justice Building, Salem, Oregon 97310, represented
Respondent.
On June 8, 1995, Richard R. Trotts filed this appeal against the Oregon
State Hospital (OSH). As clarified in a June 15, 1995 letter to this Board, Trotts alleges
that OSH violated ORS 240.309 by employing him in a temporary position
continuously for more than twenty months, by employing him as a temporary employee
filling a vacant permanent position, by failing to file the required documents concerning
extensions of his employment beyond six months, and by denying him permanent status
because of his temporary position.
The matter was investigated and set for hearing. Before the hearing, the
parties were advised of their Administrative Procedure Act rights. At the hearing, the
parties presented evidence and argued their positions.
The issue is whether OSH violated ORS 240.309 as alleged in the appeal,
and if so, what is the appropriate remedy.
Having the full record before it, this Board makes the following:
RULINGS
I. On August 22, 1995, OSH filed a motion to dismiss the appeal,
contending that the appeal was not timely filed and that Trotts had not complied with
procedural prerequisites before filing the appeal. During a prehearing conference before
the start of the hearing, the ALJ told the parties that he would defer ruling on the motion
until issuance of his recommended decision. The motion to dismiss is denied.
OSH contends that the appeal is untimely for two reasons: ( 1) Department
of Administrative Services (DAS) Policy 40.025.01 requires an employee to file a
complaint with the agency head within 15 days of the date of an alleged violation of
ORS 240.309, and Trotts did not file such a complaint; and (2) DAS Policy 40.025.01
and Board Rule 115-45-017 require an employee to file an appeal to this Board within
15 days of receipt of the final decision of the agency head, and Trotts did not fulfill that
requirement. Neither argument is persuasive.
Unlike the rules governing most management service appeals and
miscellaneous personnel actions-OAR 115-45-023, 115-45-024 and 115-45-020-the
rule governing temporary appointment appeals does not specifically require exhaustion
of internal agency appeals. Rather, it states that an appeal must be filed with this Board
within 15 days after the appellant receives the "final decision of the Agency Head."
Under that rule, an appellant may file an appeal directly with this Board as Trotts did
in this case. After he received the "final decision" of the appointing authority removing
him from his temporary position, he was entitled to file this appeal.
Our interpretation of OAR 115-45-017 is also consistent with our
construction of similar language in other Board rules. In William Rodriguez v. Secretary of
State, Case Nos. MA-24/25/34-95 (September 1995), we determined that OAR
115-45-015 (which requires that a classified employee appeal a position allocation to this
board within 15 days "after receiving the final decision of the appointing authority") did
not require exhaustion of an internal agency grievance procedure. We concluded that the
"final decision" referred to in this rule was the decision of the appointing authority
- 2 -
regarding the position allocation, not the appointing authority's «final decision" on a
grievance concerning the position allocation.
Trotts complied with this Board's rules in filing his appeal. His failure to
comply with procedural requirements imposed by DAS policies does not affect our
jurisdiction to consider his appeal. Trotts' appeal is properly before us.
2. The ALfs other rulings were reviewed and are correct.
FINDINGS OF FACT
1. In October 1993, Richard R Trotts was hired by OSH in a
temporary position as a.mental health therapy technician (MHTT). At the time he was
hired, Trotts was told that his employment would terminate on April 18, 1994.
relevant part:
2. State Policy 40.025.01, effective August 1, 1994, provides in
" ( c) A temporary employee, other than filling in behind an
employee on approved leave, shall not work beyond
the equivalent of 6 months ( 1040 hours) in a
12-month period unless an extension has been
granted. The agency head shall have delegated
authority to extend a temporary appointment when all
three of the following conditions are met:
"(A) the work to be performed continues and is the
same work performed as at the time of initial
appointment; and
"(B) no other reasonable means exist to meet the
situation; and
"(C) a process is in place to report extensions to the
Human Resource Management Division within
10 calendar days from date of approval. Form
PD 412A, Approval to Extend a Temporary
Appointment, an addendum to this policy,
fulfills the substantive information to be
reported."
- 3 -
3. After April 18, 1994, Trotts continued to work at OSH as an MHTT
in temporary positions until June 2, 1995.
During this period of temporary employment, Trotts worked in a number
of different assignments. The primary reason for Trotts' employment was the need to
maintain appropriate staffing levels at OSH so that patients would receive adequate care.
On 12 occasions Trotts' work was needed because there were vacant permanent positions
on a ward, and on 5 occasions Trotts' work was needed because employees were on leave.
Mary McBride, Associate Nursing Director for Forensic Services, placed
Trotts in each of his different assignments and notified him of these assignments by
letter. McBride believed that the employment of Trotts and other temporary workers was
the only way that appropriate staffing levels could be maintained at OSH.
OSH never filed a Form PD 412A with the Human Resource Management
Division to report the extension of Trotts' assignments as a temporary employee.
4. Sometime during December 1994 or January 1995, Trotts spoke
with OSH Personnel Officer Laura White regarding a permanent position at OSH.
White checked Trotts' records and found that he had taken the test to qualify for a
permanent MHTT position in the past but had not received a score high enough to
qualify him for placement on the list of applicants eligible for consideration for vacant
MHTT positions. White told Trotts that he should take the MHTT test again, because
he would probably get a higher score on the test since he had experience working as a
MHTT in temporary positions.
Trotts did not take the MHTT test again. He did apply for a position as a
mental health therapist I, a position which required more skill and experience than that
required for a MHTT position. Trotts was not selected for a mental health therapist I
job.
5. By letter dated January 26, 1995, McBride informed Trotts that he
needed to give her proof by March I that he held Certified Nursing Assistant (CNA)
certification or had begun to tal,e the course needed to obtain this certificate. McBride
said that CNA certification was necessary to continue working as a temporary or
permanent status employee in the Forensic Hospital Treatment Services program at
OSH. Trotts did not have CNA certification and never obtained this certification during
his period of employment at OSH.
- 4 -
CNA certification is required for many positions at OSH. An applicant for
a permanent position at OSH will also receive a higher score on the employment test if
he or she has CNA certification.
6. On June 2, 1995, Trotts was dismissed from his temporary
employment at OSH. 1
dispute.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
1. This Board has jurisdiction over the parties and subject matter of this
2. OSH did not violate ORS 240.309.
ORS 240.309 provides, in relevant part:
"(4) Employment of a temporary employee for the
same workload need, other than for leave, may not exceed
six calendar months. The decision to extend the period of
employment may be delegated by the Personnel Division of
the Oregon Department of Administrative Services to other
state agencies. Approval to extend shall be allowed only upon
an appointing authority's finding that the original emergency
continues to exist and that there is no other reasonable
means to meet the emergency. Agency actions under this
subsection are subject to post-audit review by the Oregon
Department of Administrative Services as provided in ORS
240.311.
"(5) Employment of a temporary employee for
different workload needs shall not exceed the equivalent of
six calendar months in a 12-month period.
"(6) A temporary employee shall not be denied
permanent work because of the temporary status. * * *"
1 After consulting with Maiy Jo Sikorra, OSH Director of Employee Relations, McBride
made the decision to terminate Trotts because of problems reported by Trotts' direct supervisor.
No evidence was presented regarding the nature or extent of Trotts' problems.
- 5 -
According to Appellant, OSH violated this statutory proV1s10n by
employing him in a temporary position for more than 20 months, by failing to file the
appropriate forms necessary to report the extension of his temporary employment and
by denying him a permanent job due to his temporary status. We address each of these
arguments in tum.
OSH admits that Appellant was employed as a temporary MHTT worker
for more than 20 months, but contends that Trotts' employment was lawful under the
statute. In accordance with ORS 240.309(4), the Personnel Division of Department of
Administrative Services has delegated authority to OSH to extend temporary
employment. McBride, an OSH supervisor, believed that an emergency existed-the
need for adequate staffing levels to maintain appropriate patient care-and that the only
reasonable method to deal with this emergency was to hire temporary workers such as
Trotts. Appellant introduced no evidence to demonstrate that McBride's conclusions
regarding the need to employ temporary workers was in any way mistaken or arbitrary.
OSH thus demonstrated that it met the substantive requirements for employing Trotts
as a temporary worker beyond the six month period.
OSH admits, however, that it failed to comply with the procedural
requirement of Personnel Policy 40.025.0l(l)(c)(C), because it never filed Form
PD 412A to report the extension of Trotts' temporary employment at the hospital. We
do not find that Trotts' employment was unlawful because of OSH's failure to file this
form, however.
ORS 240.309 contains no requirement that temporary employment must
be reported to Department of Administrative Services: the statute requires only that
DAS exercise post-audit review over the agency action to extend temporary employment.
The requirement that Form PD 412A be filed to report an appointing agency's action is
contained in the rule adopted by DAS's Human Resource Management Division. This
Board has no authority to set aside an_ action taken with regard to a temporary employee
simply because it violates a personnel rule. (See Knutzen v. Department of Insurance and
Finance, 129 Or App 565, 572, 879 P2d 1335 (1994) (Board has no authority to set
aside the layoff of a management service employee because the action violated the
employer's policy regarding layoff).
Nor does the evidence establish that Appellant was denied a permanent
position because of his temporary employment. Instead, the record demonstrates that
Appellant never obtained a score high enough to place him on the list of applicants
eligible for permanent positions, in spite of the advice offered by OSH Personnel
Director White.
- 6 -
Appellant's employment as a temporary worker at OSH did not violate
ORS 240.309. _The appeal is dismissed.
ORDER
The appeal is dismissed.
DATED this \,-day of October 1995.
Daniel C. Ellis, Chairman

title: UP-024-15 Board Order — Oregon School Employees Association (OSEA) v. North Santiam School District
text:
1
EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS BOARD
OF THE
STATE OF OREGON
Case No. UP-024-15
(UNFAIR LABOR PRACTICE)
OREGON SCHOOL EMPLOYEES )
ASSOCIATION, )

Complainant, ) RULINGS,

v. ) CONCLUSIONS OF LAW,
) AND ORDER
NORTH SANTIAM SCHOOL DISTRICT, ))

Sarah K. Drescher, Tedesco Law Group, Portland, Oregon, represented the Complainant.
Kelly D. Noor, Garrett Hemann Robertson P.C., Salem, Oregon, represented the Respondent.
__________________________________
On June 7, 2016, Administrative Law Judge Martin Kehoe issued a recommended order in
this matter. The parties had 14 days from the date of service in which to file written objections.
See OAR 115-010-0090; OAR 115-035-0050(2). No objections were filed.
When neither party objects to a recommended order, we generally adopt the recommended
order as our final order, and we consider any objections that could have been made to that order
unpreserved and waived. International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, Local Union No. 659
v. Eugene Water & Electric Board, Case No. UP-008-13, 25 PECBR 901 (2014). Consistent with
that practice, we will adopt the recommended order as our final order in this matter. The final order
is binding on, and has precedential value for, the named parties only. Id. Despite the precedential
limitations of such a final order, we publish the uncontested recommended order as an attachment
to the final order. Clackamas County Peace Officers Association and Atkeson v. City of West Linn,
Case No. UP-014-13, 26 PECBR 1 (2014).
ORDER
1. The Board adopts the recommended order as the final order in this matter.
2
2. The complaint is dismissed.
Dated June 30, 2016.
__________________________________________
Kathryn A. Logan, Chair

*Jason M. Weyand, Member

Adam L. Rhynard, Member
*Member Weyand Dissenting
Because neither party filed objections, my colleagues have elected to adopt the
recommended order as final consistent with the approach the Board adopted in International
Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, Local No. 659 v. Eugene Water & Electric Board, Case No.
UP-008-13, 25 PECBR 901 (2014) (EWEB). However, in EWEB, I dissented from the majority’s
decision to utilize this procedure, stating that I would not agree to adopt recommended orders that
I felt incorrectly apply the Public Employee Collective Bargaining Act. I believe this is such a
case. Rather, I would have concluded that there was a change in the status quo and that the
Respondent violated ORS 243.672(1)(e) when it refused to bargain with Complainant before
making the change. Therefore, I respectfully dissent from the order above.

Jason M. Weyand, Member

3
EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS BOARD
OF THE
STATE OF OREGON
Case No. UP-024-15
(UNFAIR LABOR PRACTICE)
OREGON SCHOOL EMPLOYEES )

NORTH SANTIAM SCHOOL DISTRICT, ))

A hearing was held before Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) Martin Kehoe on March 7, 2016 in
Salem, Oregon. The record closed on April 15, 2016, upon receipt of the parties’ post-hearing
briefs.
Sarah K. Drescher, Tedesco Law Group, Portland, Oregon, represented the Complainant.
Kelly D. Noor, Garrett Hemann Robertson P.C., Salem, Oregon, represented the Respondent.
__________________________________
On September 9, 2015, the Complainant, the Oregon School Employees Association
(OSEA), filed an unfair labor practice complaint with the Board against the Respondent, the
North Santiam School District (District). That complaint was later amended on
February 26, 2016. The issue currently presented is: (1) Did the District fail to bargain in good
faith with the OSEA in violation of ORS 243.672(1)(e) by refusing to bargain over its decision to
reduce working days and the impacts of that decision, and (2) if so, what is the appropriate
remedy? As set forth below, we conclude that the District did not violate ORS 243.672(1)(e).
4
RULINGS
All rulings of the ALJ were reviewed and are correct.
FINDINGS OF FACT
1. The District is and has been a “public employer” within the meaning of
ORS 243.650(20). It currently manages and provides services for several public schools
including Mari-Linn Elementary School, Stayton Elementary School, Stayton
Intermediate/Middle School, Stayton High School, and Sublimity School. The District’s Food
Service department also provides services for Regis High School, a private Catholic school.
2. Andrew Gardner is the District’s superintendent. Teri Butler serves as the director
of the District’s Human Resources department. Toni Silbernagel is the director of Food Service.
3. The OSEA is and has been a “labor organization” within the meaning of
ORS 243.650(13). It is the exclusive representative of a bargaining unit that includes a variety of
classified District employees. That group includes, in part, a number of employees who work for
Food Service.
4. The OSEA and the District have been parties to a series of collective bargaining
agreements (CBAs). Every one of those CBAs has included a “reopening clause” that allows the
CBA to be modified each spring upon the mutual consent of both the OSEA and the District.
5. The District gives each of its employees a personalized work calendar with a
specific number of workdays prior to the start of every school year. None of the parties’ CBAs
have specified exactly how many days should be included in a given calendar or addressed
reductions in workdays. Moreover, reductions in workdays were not discussed during the
negotiations that led up to the parties’ most recent CBA, which is effective from July 1, 2013
through June 30, 2017.
6. In practice, the total number of days included in any District employee’s work
calendar can vary by position and department and may increase or decrease from one school year
to the next. That is also true for Food Service employees. Nevertheless, when a Food Service
employee is assigned less than 185 days for a particular school year, it is often colloquially
described as a “cut” in workdays.
7. Food Service employees had their work calendars reduced from 185 days in the
2003-2004, 2007-2008, 2008-2009, 2010-2011, 2014-2015, and 2015-2016 school years. The
2003-2004, 2007-2008, 2008-2009, and 2010-2011 reductions were made unilaterally and
without a demand to bargain.
8. To determine how many days work calendars will include each year, the District
typically considers its current and projected finances, costs, and what services are required for
each campus. It also tries to maintain employees’ benefits levels. Occasionally, the District has
asked its employees or the OSEA for input. Food Service employee calendars are ultimately
5
determined by the collaborative efforts of Director Silbernagel, Human Resources, and
Superintendent Gardner.
9. Most Food Service employees work exclusively during the regular school year
and are not required to work during the summer months when school is out. However, any
District employee can choose to complete a special application and compete for extra work
through the District’s summer food program.
10. Most Food Service employees have historically chosen not to participate in the
summer food program, as they often have separate summer jobs or other obligations.
Nevertheless, some Food Service employees have participated in the program in the past.
11. When Food Service employees do apply for the summer food program, they are
given a hiring preference because they would already have the experience necessary to perform
the work. However, if a Food Service employee is ultimately hired for summer work, he or she is
not guaranteed a particular number of hours.
12. In addition to the summer food program, Food Service employees can also take
advantage of other opportunities to work extra hours during the normal school year. Those
include working substitute hours. The District cannot know how many or which substitute hours
will be available in advance of the school year. The number of substitute hours that do become
available fluctuates from year to year.
13. Food Service is partially funded by the federal government and does not receive
funds from the District’s general fund. During the 2013-2014 school year, Food Service was
faced with new federal laws that required that healthier, more expensive foods be served and led
to a significant increase in costs.
14. On May 5, 2014, the District received the results of an audit of Food Service that
had been conducted by an outside, third-party consultant. Among other things, the audit urged
Food Service “to consider a restructuring to reduce the number of the job levels and the number
of managers.” It also suggested that “[t]he district might want to consider assigning some
secretarial time to the food service department to relieve the director from the paper work burden
and allow her to go to schools more often.” (Exh. C-8 at 2.)
15. Negotiations for the parties’ 2014 “reopener” began with a May 14, 2014
bargaining session. In that first session, Superintendent Gardner announced that the District
would be sharing the results of the Food Service audit with the OSEA’s bargaining team during
the next session. Additionally, both parties proposed several unrelated contractual changes.
16. During the second bargaining session, which occurred on May 19, 2014, the
District gave the OSEA a copy of the audit results. Director Butler also announced that the
District would be proposing reducing Food Service employees’ calendar days and having those
employees make up for their lost days by working during the summer months. At that point, Jedd
Rivera, an OSEA field representative, responded that reductions in calendar days could not be
unilaterally implemented and would need to be negotiated. In support of his position, Rivera
6
mentioned the Board’s order in Oregon School Employees Association v. Parkrose School
District, Case No. UP-030-12, 25 PECBR 783 (2013). The District then indicated that it
disagreed with that position.
17. The third bargaining session occurred on May 27, 2014. In that session, the
District shared what it saw as three possible approaches for balancing its budget and
implementing some of the changes recommended by the Food Service audit. After the OSEA
heard those approaches, it indicated that it did not like any of them and said that it would need
more time to review them.
18. Under the District’s first approach, labeled Plan A, four Food Service employees
would have lost ten workdays and three others would have lost two days. The second approach,
Plan B, involved reducing Food Service employees’ benefits and pay. The third approach, Plan
C, would have required Food Service employees to work during the summer.
19. On May 29, 2014, the OSEA took the three plans to its members, who ultimately
voted in favor of Plan A, but also expressed a desire to reduce the number of days that would be
cut. Specifically, they proposed: (1) “The four (4) food service workers that the district proposed
ten (10) days reduction shall only be reduced five (5) days,” and (2) “The three (3) food service
workers that the district proposed to be reduced by two (2) days shall only be reduced by one (1)
day.” (Exh. C-19 at 1.)
20. On June 2, 2014, Rivera sent Superintendent Gardner an email that included a
copy of an arbitrator’s opinion and award (dated May 28, 2013) that resulted from a dispute
between the OSEA and the Sweet Home School District. That same day, the District sent the
OSEA a copy of a letter stating that one bargaining unit employee’s work calendar was being
reduced from 185 days to 180 days.
21. A fourth bargaining session occurred on June 3, 2014. During that session, Rivera
presented the members’ modified version of Plan A. The District then replied that it preferred
Plan C and did not actually want the OSEA to choose a plan. In addition, the District said that it
could simply have implemented any of the plans if it wanted to do so, and indicated that it had
not given up its managerial right to assign workdays.
22. The fifth and final bargaining session for the 2014 reopener occurred on
June 10, 2014. In that session, the District initially attempted to show that Plan C was the
preferable option. However, the OSEA disagreed with that and reiterated that it wanted a
modified version of Plan A. The District then repeated that it could simply choose a plan and that
it was not up to the OSEA to choose. Later, the District proposed its own modified version of
Plan A that included fewer cuts than the District had originally suggested. The OSEA tentatively
agreed to that arrangement.
23. By June 18, 2014, each of the parties had signed a memorandum of understanding
(MOU) memorializing their June 10, 2014 agreement. On June 25, 2014, the OSEA’s members
voted unanimously in favor of ratifying the MOU.
7
24. The MOU specifically provides, “[T]he positions that were originally slated for a
ten (10) day cut, will now be reduced by six (6) work days. Those positions that were slated for a
five (5) day and two (2) day cut will remain at five (5) and (2) day reduction.” (Exh. J-2 at 1.)
The MOU does not overtly address how long that arrangement would remain in effect.
Moreover, prior to signing the MOU, the parties had never discussed that issue.
25. The next round of reopener negotiations (conducted in advance of the 2015-2016
school year) started in early June 2015 and ended around July 17, 2015, when the parties signed
a formal tentative agreement. The subject of reducing Food Service employees’ workdays was
not openly addressed by either party during that reopener period. The parties likewise did not
discuss the MOU signed the year before.
26. On July 21, 2015, the District sent out letters stating that certain Food Service
positions would be cut days. The cuts that were to be made in the 2015-2016 school year were
the same cuts that had been made in the 2014-2015 year. In essence, the District would be
carrying over the terms of the parties’ 2014 MOU.
27. On July 23, 2015, the OSEA sent the District a letter notifying it that the OSEA
desired to negotiate regarding the District’s decision to reduce hours and days in the Food
Service department.
28. On August 3, 2015, the District sent the OSEA a response referencing Articles
4.1, 6.3, and 6.7 of the parties’ 2013-2017 CBA. The response also argued that the District’s
actions were consistent with the parties’ past practice and the status quo.
29. Article 4.1(1)(c) of the 2013-2017 CBA provides, “The District retains the right to
assign, schedule and direct the work of an employee within any given job title in accordance
with the terms of this agreement.” (Exh. J-1 at 7.) Article 6.3 states, “Employees hours per day
shall be assigned at the discretion of the District. The building administrator or director
(whichever is appropriate), shall notify employees of the hours worked per day at the beginning
of the school year.” (Exh. J-1 at 9.) Article 6.7 states, “The District will notify less than
twelve-month (12) employees before the start of their work year as to the number of workdays to
be included in the employee work calendar. Additional workdays may be scheduled as requested
by the building administrator or director (whichever is appropriate), and approved by the
Superintendent.” (Exh. J-1 at 9.)
30. On August 7, 2015, the OSEA sent a new letter to the District stating that the
OSEA desired to negotiate regarding the District’s decision to reduce hours and days in Food
Service as well as the impact of that decision.
31. On August 20, 2015, two of the parties’ representatives met in person and
discussed the District’s planned reduction in hours and workdays. During that meeting, the
District continued to argue that it had a managerial right to reduce employees’ workdays and
accordingly did not need to negotiate that issue. It further suggested that employees who lost
hours could make up for those hours by working substitute hours or working during the summer.
8
32. On August 21, 2015, the District gave the OSEA another response that repeated
the arguments the District made in its August 3, 2015 letter. The response also repeated the
District’s suggestion regarding working during the summer, but added that all Food Service staff
would also have the opportunity to increase the number of workdays via additional work related
to a new YMCA after school program.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
1. This Board has jurisdiction over the parties and the subject matter of this dispute.
2. The District did not violate ORS 243.672(1)(e).
Legal Standards
The OSEA’s complaint contends that the District violated ORS 243.672(1)(e), which
prohibits a public employer from refusing to bargain collectively in good faith with the
bargaining representative of its employees. Under the Public Employee Collective Bargaining
Act, the public employer’s duty to bargain is limited to changes to employment conditions that
are deemed “mandatory subjects of bargaining.” For other, “permissive” subjects, the public
employer is free to bargain or not to bargain. However, if a change to a permissive subject has an
impact on a mandatory subject, the public employer may also be required to bargain regarding
that impact. Three Rivers Ed. Assoc. v. Three Rivers Sch. Dist., 254 Or App 570, 574, 294 P3d
547 (2013) (citations omitted).
If the subject in dispute is specifically included in the definition of “employment
relations” under ORS 243.650(7)(a), then the subject is mandatory for bargaining. According to
that subsection, employment relations “includes, but is not limited to, matters concerning direct
or indirect monetary benefits, hours, vacations, sick leave, grievance procedures and other
conditions of employment.” Subjects defined in ORS 243.650(7)(b), (d), (e), (f), and (g) are
permissive. To determine the status of subjects the PECBA does not designate as mandatory or
permissive, we use the balancing test set forth in ORS 243.650(7)(c). Under that test, a subject is
permissive if the impact of the subject on management’s prerogatives is greater than the impact
on employees’ wages, hours, or other conditions of employment. Portland Fire Fighters Assoc.
v. City of Portland, 305 Or 275, 282-85, 751 P2d 770 (1988); Oregon AFSCME Council 75 v.
State of Oregon, Department of Public Safety Standards and Training, Case No. UP-56-99, 19
PECBR 76, 89-92 (2001).
Whenever an unlawful unilateral change is alleged, we first identify the status quo and
determine whether the employer changed it. If the employer did change the status quo, we then
decide whether the change concerns a mandatory bargaining subject. Lebanon Education
Association/OEA v. Lebanon Community School District, Case No. UP-4-06, 22 PECBR 323,
360 (2008). To determine the status quo, we often look to a variety of sources including the
terms of a CBA or other memorialized polices or work rules. In other cases, the status quo can
simply be the product of an employer’s pattern of behavior. See Oregon AFSCME Council 75,
Local 2831 v. Lane County Human Resources Division, Case No. UP-22-04, 20 PECBR 987,
993-95 (2005); Coos Bay Police Officers’ Association v. City of Coos Bay and Coos Bay Police
Department, Case No. UP-61-92, 14 PECBR 229, 233 (1993), citing East County Bargaining
9
Council (David Douglas Education Association) v. David Douglas School District, Case No.
UP-84-86, 9 PECBR 9184, 9192 n 11 (1986).
A past practice is generally characterized by clarity and consistency, repetition over a
long period of time, acceptability to both parties, and mutuality. Lane County Human Resources
Division, 20 PECBR at 993-95. Further, a labor agreement is a type of contract, and
unambiguous contracts must be enforced according to their terms. See Yogman v. Parrott, 325
Or 358, 361, 937 P2d 1019 (1997); Eagle Industries, Inc. v. Thompson, 321 Or 398, 405, 900
P2d 475 (1995); Oregon School Employees Association, Chapter 89 v. Rainier School Dist. No.
13, 311 Or 188, 194, 808 P2d 83 (1991). As a general rule, parties are strictly bound to
agreements they have signed and this Board will not rewrite or reconstitute the language of those
agreements. Gresham Grade School Teachers Association v. Gresham Grade School District No.
4 and Larson, Case No. C-184-78, 5 PECBR 2889, 2895 (1980), remanded for further
proceedings on other matters, 52 Or App 881, 630 P2d 1304 (1981), order on remand, 6 PECBR
4953 (1981).
As the complainant in this contested case, the OSEA bears the burden of proving its
alleged violations by a preponderance of the evidence. ORS 183.450(2); Gallant v. Board of
Medical Examiners, 159 Or App 175, 180, 974 P2d 814 (1999); Ralphs v. OPEU and State of
Oregon, Executive Department, Case No. UP-68-69-91, 15 PECBR 115, 118 (1994). The party
alleging a status quo based on a past practice has the burden of proving its establishment.
Amalgamated Transit Union, Division 757 v. Tri-County Metropolitan District of Oregon, Case
No. UP-62-05, 22 PECBR 911, recons, 23 PECBR 34 (2009); Lane County Human Resources
Division, 20 PECBR at 993.
DISCUSSION
The OSEA asserts, in short, that the applicable past practice and status quo for Food
Service’s classified employees was a 185-day work calendar with a requirement that all
reductions in workdays must be bargained. In our view, that position is largely unsupported by
the evidence presented, which indicates that, historically, the number of calendar days a Food
Service employee is required to work has quite often varied from one year to the next. Although
there is admittedly some evidence of an informal 185-day “baseline” for many Food Service
positions, it is quite clear that that number has never truly been fixed. The record also shows that,
for all of the relevant calendar changes save one, the cuts that the District made were not
negotiated. It follows, therefore, that the practice and status quo identified by the OSEA has not
been “clearly established” as our precedent requires. See Lane County Human Resources
Division, 20 PECBR at 993.
The OSEA contends that the status quo cannot, as the District suggests, be one of
unilateral variability, for that practice has not been sufficiently clear, consistent, or long-lived. In
support of that argument, the OSEA essentially points to the 2014 MOU and the negotiations that
led up to it. On that subject, we would grant that that example shows that the District has not
always made cuts to workdays unilaterally. Nonetheless, one isolated instance does not
necessarily establish a status quo. See Gresham Police Officers Association v. City of Gresham,
Case No. UP-06/18-09, 24 PECBR 55, 71 (2010); McKenzie Education Association/Lane
10
Unified Bargaining Council/OEA v. McKenzie School District 68, Case No. UP-81-94, 16
PECBR 156, 164 (1995). As noted, to be properly established, a practice must ordinarily occur
repetitively over a long period of time. Lane County Human Resources Division, 20 PECBR at
993. Under these circumstances, one could reasonably argue that the parties’ one instance of
bargaining cuts in 2014 is outweighed by the other changes in the record, which include similar
cuts to days, made unilaterally and without complaint, in 2003, 2007, 2008, and 2010.
At the same time, an even more compelling and ultimately dispositive argument can be
made that, if the 2014 MOU is in fact a memorialization of the parties’ negotiated-for status quo
as the OSEA suggests, then the District, by simply maintaining the cuts of that agreement for
another year, has not actually changed anything without bargaining. As the OSEA notes, the
MOU “is devoid of any durational language.” Although either party could argue that it only
meant for the MOU to last one school year, subjective intentions or unspoken understandings
and assumptions do not control. City of Portland v. The District Council of Trade Unions, Case
Nos. UP-58/76-87, 10 PECBR 109, 118 (1987). Put simply, we are not convinced that the plain
text of the MOU is ambiguous. Accordingly, we need not consult extrinsic or parol evidence in
this case, and we will not insert or read in qualifiers – including a duration – that the parties did
not include. See Independent Association of Linn-Benton Community College Classified
Employees v. Linn-Benton Community College, Case No. UP-029-13, 26 PECBR 51, 55-57
(June 2014); AFSCME Local 189 v. City of Portland (Portland Police Bureau), Case No.
UP-49-08, 26 PECBR 62, 638-39 (January 2012).
The OSEA separately argues that the plain language of Articles 4 and 6.7 of the current
CBA does not, as the District argues, give the District the unfettered authority to unilaterally cut
workdays. However, even if the OSEA’s contract interpretation were correct, it would do very
little to establish the past practice or status quo that the OSEA has outlined and thus does not
help the OSEA meet its initial burden. Moreover, we conclude that it is at least equally as true
that the CBA does not expressly state that the District cannot unilaterally change calendars each
year and does not specify precisely how many workdays should be included in them as a default.
In that way, the facts of the instant case can be meaningfully distinguished from those of Oregon
School Employees Association v. Parkrose District, Case No. UP-030-12, 25 PECBR 783,
recons, 25 PECBR 845 (2013), for example, wherein the parties’ contract actually set forth a
negotiated number of workdays for different classified employees. See also Eugene Police
Employees’ Association v. City of Eugene, Case Nos. UP-38/41-08, 23 PECBR 972, 996-97
(2010) (no status quo established by agreements that neither prohibited nor addressed
complained-of action). We further note that a breach of contract, in and of itself, does not violate

text:
1
EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS BOARD
OF THE
STATE OF OREGON
Case No. FR-001-17
(UNFAIR LABOR PRACTICE)
S.R.,
Complainant,
v.
AFSCME Local 328,
Respondent.
)

))))

DISMISSAL ORDER
S.R., Portland, Oregon, appeared pro se.
Jennifer K. Chapman, Legal Counsel, Oregon AFSCME, represented Respondent.
__________________________
On September 1, 2017, Complainant filed an unfair labor practice complaint against AFSCME Local 328 (AFSCME). The case was assigned to Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) Julie D. Reading.
In her complaint, Complainant alleged that her employer, Oregon Health Sciences University (OHSU), initiated termination proceedings against her, and that she was represented by AFSCME during that process. On March 3, 2017, Complainant signed a settlement agreement in which she agreed to voluntarily resign in exchange for compensation and other consideration from OHSU. Complainant claims that AFSCME violated its duty of fair representation by declining to pursue a grievance on her behalf, by pressuring her to enter into the settlement agreement, and by failing to negotiate an adequate settlement.
ALJ Reading investigated the complaint to determine if an issue of fact or law exists that warrants a hearing, as required by OAR 115-035-0005. By letter dated October 12, 2017, ALJ Reading issued Complainant an Order to Show Cause, informing Complainant of several bases for dismissal of her complaint: 1) her complaint appeared to be untimely; 2) her claim appeared to be contractually barred by her settlement agreement because she waived her right to pursue any actions against OHSU or AFSCME, including a duty of fair representation claim; 3) Complainant was incorrect that the AFSCME-OHSU collective bargaining agreement entitled her to more compensation than she received as part of her settlement agreement; and 4) Complainant failed to identify which provisions of the Public Employee Collective Bargaining Act (PECBA) that 2
AFSCME allegedly violated, as required by this Board’s rules. ALJ Reading gave Complainant until October 20, 2017, to withdraw the complaint or provide reasons why the complaint should not be dismissed despite its untimeliness and pleading deficiencies.
Complainant responded to the Order to Show Cause on October 20, 2017. She provided more detail regarding her factual allegations and submitted additional documentary evidence, including a copy of electronic communications between Complainant and the AFSCME representative who assisted her during the settlement negotiations. After reviewing Complainant’s response, ALJ Reading recommended to this Board that we dismiss her complaint without a hearing.
In considering whether Complainant’s complaint presents an issue of fact or law that requires a hearing, we assume that the facts alleged in the complaint are true. Schroeder v. State of Oregon, Department of Corrections, Oregon State Correctional Institution and Association of Oregon Correctional Employees, Case Nos. UP-49/50-98, 17 PECBR 907 (1999). We may also rely on undisputed facts discovered during our investigation of the complaint. Upton v. Oregon Education Association/Uniserv, Case No. UP-58-06 at 2, 21 PECBR 867, 868 (2007).
We have considered the complaint and the submissions of the parties. We summarize the alleged or undisputed facts as follows:
1. On February 7, 2017, OHSU issued Complainant a pre-discharge letter, alleging a serious basis for discharge.
2. On or about February 16, 2017, OHSU notified Complainant that her employment would be terminated.
3. On February 21, 2017, Complainant informed her AFSCME representative that she wished to pursue a grievance disputing her termination.
4. AFSCME declined to pursue a grievance on Complainant’s behalf, and instead engaged in settlement negotiations with OHSU.1
5. The AFSCME representative communicated OHSU’s final offer to Complainant on February 21, 2017.
6. On February 24, 2017, Complainant responded to the AFSCME representative, stating that she would “take” the offer and wanted to “move on.” Complainant thanked the AFSCME representative.
1At this stage of the case, AFSCME has not yet been given the opportunity to file an answer indicating whether it admits or denies Complainant’s allegation that AFSCME declined to pursue a grievance, and we are not making such a finding of fact based on the record of an evidentiary hearing. Rather, we are assuming that all of Complainant’s specific factual allegations, including this allegation, are true, solely for the purpose of determining whether this case should be dismissed without a hearing. 3
7. On March 3, 2017, Complainant contacted the AFSCME representative and asked to meet so that she could sign the separation agreement, again stating that she was “ready to move on.”
8. OHSU, AFSCME, and Complainant are parties to a “Separation Agreement and General Release” (Separation Agreement). Complainant signed the Separation Agreement on March 3, 2017. In the Separation Agreement, OHSU agreed to provide Complainant with 16 weeks of severance pay and other benefits, including extended health coverage, in exchange for Complainant’s voluntary resignation and a release of liability.
9. The Separation Agreement included a general release, in which Complainant agreed to release OHSU and AFSCME from any and all liability relating to Complainant’s employment or association with OHSU or the termination thereof.
10. The Separation Agreement also required Complainant and AFSCME to “withdraw any and all grievances filed against OHSU on behalf of” Complainant.
11. On March 13 and 15, 2017, Complainant and the AFSCME representative exchanged text messages regarding when Complainant could pick up her settlement check.
12. Some months later, Complainant determined that the AFSCME-OHSU collective bargaining agreement provides for certain severance benefits. To be eligible for those benefits, an employee must be “involuntarily terminated due to program closure, position elimination or reorganization,” and meet other requirements. Believing that those benefits applied to her, Complainant filed this unfair labor practice complaint, asserting that the Separation Agreement provided less benefits than the severance benefits outlined in the collective bargaining agreement.
DISCUSSION
We dismiss the complaint on two grounds: (1) failure to state a cause of action, and (2) contractual waiver.
Complainant claims that AFSCME violated ORS 243.672(2)(a), which is the provision of PECBA that requires the exclusive representative of a group of employees to represent all employees in the bargaining unit fairly. Griffin v. Service Employees International Union Local 503, Oregon Public Employees Union and State of Oregon, Employment Department, Case No. FR-02-09 at 24, 24 PECBR 1, 24 (2010).
When reviewing duty of fair representation claims, this Board has long held that a labor organization’s actions and decisions as the exclusive representative of employees must be afforded broad discretion. See Caddy and Van Hooser v. Multnomah County Deputy Sheriff’s Association, Case No. C-62-84 at 10-11, 7 PECBR 6545, 6554-55 (1984) (citing Ford Motor Co. v. Huffman, 345 U.S. 330, 31 LRRM 2548 (1953)); see also Conger v. Jackson County and Oregon Public Employees Union, Case No. UP-22-98 at 10, 18 PECBR 79, 88 (1999). We will find a violation of subsection (2)(a) only where a labor organization’s actions are arbitrary, discriminatory, or taken in bad faith. Chan v. Leach and Stubblefield, Clackamas County Community College; Brown, Clackamas Community College Association of Classified Employees, OEA/NEA, Case No. UP-13-05 at 12, 21 PECBR 563, 574 (2006). A union’s action is arbitrary if it lacks a rational 4
basis. Id. A union’s conduct is discriminatory if there is “substantial evidence of discrimination that is intentional, severe, and unrelated to legitimate union objectives.” Id. at 13; 21 PECBR at 575. A union’s conduct is in bad faith if it intentionally acts against a member’s interest and does so for an improper reason. Id.
In order to proceed to a hearing, Complainant must allege facts that, if proven, would establish that AFSCME acted arbitrarily, discriminatorily, or in bad faith. If such factual allegations are not in the complaint, the complaint will be dismissed without a hearing for failure to state a claim for relief. Putvinskas v. Southwestern Oregon Community College Classified Federation, Local 3972, AFT, AFL-CIO, and Southwestern Oregon Community College, Case No. UP-71-99 at 12, 18 PECBR 882, 893 (2000). As we explain below, we dismiss this case because, even assuming that the facts alleged in the complaint are true, those facts do not establish that AFSCME acted arbitrarily, discriminatorily, or in bad faith.
Complainant’s primary claim is that AFSCME violated its duty of fair representation by negotiating an inadequate settlement agreement. That claim is premised on an allegation that Complainant received less severance pay than was contractually required under the collective bargaining agreement. Complainant, however, is relying on a severance pay provision that applies only to employees who are terminated due to a program closure, reorganization, or position elimination. That provision did not apply to Complainant because the grounds for her proposed termination were not program closure, reorganization, or position elimination. Thus, the premise of Complainant’s claim against AFSCME is incorrect, and there is no issue of fact or law warranting a hearing on this claim.
Complainant also claims that AFSCME violated its duty of fair representation by negotiating a settlement agreement instead of pursuing a grievance on her behalf. Generally, it is lawful for a union to try to settle a potential grievance instead of litigating it. As explained above, such conduct would violate ORS 243.672(2)(a) only if AFSCME acted with improper or discriminatory motives, or without a rational basis. Complainant has not alleged any facts that, if true, would establish that AFSCME’s conduct in pursuing a voluntary settlement agreement lacked a rational basis. And, because none of Complainant’s specific factual allegations tend to show that AFSCME acted with a discriminatory intent or otherwise improper motive, there is no basis for finding that AFSCME engaged in unlawful discrimination or acted in bad faith. Block v. Amalgamated Transit Union, Division 757, Case No. FR-001-15 at 5, 26 PECBR 486 (2015).2
Complainant also claims that AFSCME unfairly pressured her into entering to the Separation Agreement. However, none of the allegations about AFSCME’s conduct in the course of settlement negotiations would, even if proven, establish that AFSCME acted discriminatorily, in bad faith, or arbitrarily. For example, Complainant claims that she felt pressured to agree to the settlement because AFSCME (allegedly) decided not to pursue a grievance on her behalf. But, as discussed above, there are no factual allegations that, if proven, would establish that AFSCME
2Even if Complainant intended to allege that AFSCME stated that it would not pursue her grievance to arbitration if she declined to sign the Separation Agreement, her complaint would present no issue of fact or law that warrants a hearing, because a union has substantial discretion in negotiating grievance settlements, and may refuse to take a grievance to arbitration if the grievant rejects a reasonable settlement offer. Martin v. Portland Association of Teachers and Portland School District #1, Case No. UP-28-01 at 6, 19 PECBR 513, 518 (2001).5
made that decision for unlawful reasons or acted arbitrarily. Complainant also alleges that she felt pressured to decide whether to accept OHSU’s settlement offer quickly, but Complainant’s own evidence establishes that she took approximately three days to consider OHSU’s February 21 final offer before she accepted it, that another week passed before she actually signed the Separation Agreement, and that she repeatedly expressed her decision to accept OHSU’s settlement offer and voluntarily resign. Although we understand that Complainant is arguing that she faced difficult pressure when deciding whether to accept OHSU’s settlement offer, that pressure does not, in itself, mean that AFSCME’s alleged conduct was unlawful.3
We also dismiss this complaint because Complainant, by agreeing to the terms of the Separation Agreement, contractually waived her right to pursue any claims against OHSU or AFSCME arising from her employment with OHSU (or termination of that employment), which includes a duty of fair representation claim against AFSCME. Although Complainant claims that AFSCME pressured her into entering into the Separation Agreement, as explained above, her factual allegations, even if proven, would not establish that AFSCME’s actions were discriminatory, in bad faith, or arbitrary. As a result, there is no basis for disregarding the contractual waiver.
For all of the reasons stated above, there is no issue of fact or law that merits a hearing, and we dismiss the complaint. See ORS 243.676(1)(b).
ORDER
The complaint is dismissed.
DATED: November 20, 2017. __________________________________________
Adam L. Rhynard, Chair
__________________________________________
Lisa M. Umscheid, Member
__________________________________________
Jennifer Sung, Member
This Order may be appealed pursuant to ORS 183.482.
3We also note that Complainant’s claims that AFSCME unlawfully declined to pursue a grievance and unlawfully pressured her to enter into the Separation Agreement are untimely, and could be dismissed on that ground. Under ORS 243.672(3), a complaint must be filed “not later than 180 days following the occurrence of an unfair labor practice.” ORS 243.672(3) incorporates a discovery rule, which means that the 180-day limitation period begins to run when the complainant knows or reasonably should know that an unfair labor practice has occurred. Rogue River Education Assoc. v. Rogue River School, 244 Or App 181, 189, 260 P3d 619 (2011). In this case, Complainant knew, or reasonably should have known, that AFSCME had declined to file a grievance or pressured her to sign the Separation Agreement by the date that she signed that agreement, March 3, 2017, at the latest. Therefore, Complainant needed to file her claim by August 30, 2017. Complainant, however, filed her complaint on September 1, 2017, which means that it was untimely filed.

On October 21, 2014, this Board issued an order dismissing the complaint filed by the Laborers’ International Union of North America, Local 483 (LIUNA), which alleged that the City of Portland (City) violated ORS 243.672(1)(a), (c) and (e). 26 PECBR 269 (2014). On November 10, 2014, the City filed a petition for representation costs. On November 26, 2014, LIUNA filed objections to the petition.1
Pursuant to ORS 243.676(3)(b) and OAR 115-035-0055, this Board finds that:
1.The City filed a timely petition for representation costs, and LIUNA filed timelyobjections to the petition.
2.The City is the prevailing party. LIUNA objects to this finding, asserting that ourorder dismissing the complaint made no conclusion with respect to whether the City engaged in an unfair labor practice, which is required for an award of representation costs under ORS 243.676(3). We disagree with LIUNA’s assertion. Under ORS 243.676(3), this Board shall award representation costs after finding that a respondent has not engaged in an unfair labor practice. Here, we dismissed the complaint before hearing because LIUNA was unable to submit evidence to carry its burden of proving that the City committed the alleged unfair labor practice violations. In doing so, we made a finding (at least implicitly) that the City had not committed the
1This Board subsequently asked the City to respond to LIUNA’s objections, and the City did so on January 30, 2015. 1
alleged unfair labor practice violations. Our dismissal of this complaint is similar to other dismissals that may occur after a hearing in which a complainant has not produced sufficient evidence to meet its burden of proving the alleged unfair labor practice. Because we have found that the City did not engage in the alleged unfair labor practices, we will award the City its reasonable representation costs.
4. The City requests an award of $3,300 in representation costs, asserting that such an award represents the reasonable value of the services provided by counsel for the City. See OAR 115-035-0055(1)(c). In support of that request, the City avers that $165 per hour is a reasonable rate and estimates that over 60 hours were spent on the case, for a total of $9,900 in costs.2
5. LIUNA asserts that the affidavit submitted by counsel for the City is insufficient to support any award of representation costs. According to LIUNA, the affidavit must do more than “estimate” the total number of hours spent, but rather must break down how many hours were spent on each task.
We disagree with LIUNA’s assertion that the affidavit submitted by the City’s counsel is per se insufficient to award representation costs. Where, as here, a petitioner “was not charged fees,” the petition must include, among other things, a statement of the costs requested, supported by an affidavit that describes in detail “the basis for the amount of costs requested.” See OAR 115-035-0055(2)(b). Here, counsel for the City submitted a detailed list of the tasks performed in the case and a sworn estimation of the time spent on those tasks. The affidavit further averred that this represented the City’s customary practice of timekeeping in these matters. We find the affidavit sufficient to support the petition.
6. The City’s requested rate of $165 per hour is average. See Oregon School Employees Association v. North Clackamas School District, Case No. UP-017-13, 26 PECBR 129, 130 (2014) (Rep. Cost Order) (the average rate for representation costs is between $165 and $170 per hour). The number of hours claimed (60) is above average for a case requiring one day of hearing. See id. (cases generally require an average of 45 to 50 hours per day of hearing). However, as noted above and in our dismissal order, this case is unusual in that it was referred to this Board for a decision just before the scheduled first day of a two-day hearing. Because the two days of hearing were scheduled on consecutive days, it would be reasonable for the City’s counsel to have fully prepared for a two-day hearing at the time that the matter was referred to this Board. Under such circumstances, we find the City’s claimed 60 hours to be reasonable.
7. An average award is generally one-third of the reasonable representation costs of the prevailing party, subject to the $5,000 cap in OAR 115-035-0055(1)(a). LIUNA asserts, however, that we should award a lesser fraction of the City’s reasonable representation costs because no “finding was made exonerating the City.” As set forth above, we disagree with
2The City does not bill City bureaus at an hourly rate for labor law matters such as this, but City attorneys do complete time sheets for purposes of public accountability. Although those time sheets generally reflect the number of hours worked per day, they do not typically break down the number of hours spent per day on any particular task or case.
2
LIUNA’s characterization of our dismissal order. In short, the dismissal order “exonerated” the City of the alleged unfair labor practices in a manner similar to other dismissal orders that issue after a hearing took place. Having considered the purposes and policies of the Public Employee Collective Bargaining Act, our awards in prior cases, and the reasonable costs of services rendered, this Board awards the City representation costs of $3,300.
ORDER
LIUNA will remit $3,300 to the City within 30 days of the date of this Order.
DATED this 3 day of March, 2015.
This Order may be appealed pursuant to ORS 183.482.
